questions.lead: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, on returning to his laboratory from a holiday with his family in Suffolk: a fungus had grown on a culture plate he had left on a bench, and the staphylococci around it had been destroyed. The discovery later brought him a share of the 1945 Nobel Prize.

questions.lead: On 3 September 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a fungus on a contaminated culture plate had destroyed the bacteria around it, the observation that led to penicillin, the first antibiotic. The discovery was recognised with the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, which he shared with two other scientists.

sources.excerpt: Before leaving for his holiday, he inoculated staphylococci on culture plates and left them on a bench in a corner of his laboratory. On 3 September 1928, Fleming returned to his laboratory having spent a holiday with his family at Suffolk. On his return, Fleming noticed that one culture was contaminated with a fungus, and that the colonies of staphylococci immediately surrounding the fungus had been destroyed, whereas other staphylococci colonies farther away were normal, famously remarking "That's funny". He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain "for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases".

The Challenger Deep is the deepest known point of the seabed of Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, in the ocean territory of the Federated States of Micronesia. A 2011 study placed the depth at 5,971 ± 5 fathoms (10,920 ± 9 m; 35,826 ± 30 ft) with a 2021 study revising the value to 10,935 ± 6 m (35,876 ± 20 ft) at a 95% confidence level. The depression is named after the British Royal Navy survey ships HMS Challenger, whose expedition of 1872–1876 first located it, and HMS Challenger II, whose expedition of 1950–1952 established its record-setting depth. The first descent by any vehicle was conducted by the United States Navy using the bathyscaphe Trieste in January 1960.

The Valley of the Kings, also known as the Valley of the Gates of the Kings, is an area in Egypt where, for a period of nearly 500 years from the Eighteenth Dynasty to the Twentieth Dynasty, rock-cut tombs were excavated for pharaohs and powerful nobles under the New Kingdom of ancient Egypt. It is a wadi sitting on the west bank of the Nile, opposite Thebes (modern-day Luxor) and within the heart of the Theban Necropolis. With the 2005 discovery of a new chamber and the 2008 discovery of two further tomb entrances, the Valley of the Kings is known to contain 65 tombs and chambers, ranging in size from the simple pit that is KV54 to the complex tomb that is KV5, which alone has over 120 chambers for the sons of Ramesses II. After a systematic search, they discovered the actual tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) in November 1922. It was discovered by Howard Carter on 4 November 1922, with clearance and conservation work continuing until 1932.
